description: Recognise normal, reverse, thrust and strike-slip faults from the stresses that produce them.
content_html:
When Rocks Break Instead of Bend

In the previous lesson you saw that compressional stress can slowly bend buried rocks into folds. But rocks do not always bend — sometimes they fracture. A fault is a planar fracture along which measurable displacement has occurred. The type of fault that forms depends on the direction and nature of the stress applied to the rock.

Geologists classify faults by comparing the movement of two key blocks: the hanging wall and the footwall. Imagine standing on the fault plane itself — the block above you is the hanging wall, the block beneath your feet is the footwall. Whether the hanging wall moves up or down relative to the footwall tells you immediately which type of fault you are looking at.

Key Fact

There are four main fault types on the specification: normal, reverse, thrust, and strike-slip. Each is the product of a different type of tectonic stress — tensional, compressional, or shear.

Normal Faults — Tensional Stress

A normal fault forms when tensional stress pulls the crust apart. The hanging wall slides down relative to the footwall. Normal faults are the signature structure of divergent plate boundaries, where two plates move apart. The East African Rift Valley is a classic modern example: as the African plate is pulled apart by tensional stress, a central block drops down between parallel normal faults to form a rift valley. Fault planes in normal faults are typically steep, dipping at 60° or more.

On a geological map, you can recognise a normal fault by the displacement of rock units. A distinctive feature is that the rock sequence is repeated on either side of the fault — looking across the fault, each rock unit appears to continue but at a lower level on the downthrown side. In cross-section, the hanging wall drops, widening the exposure of younger surface rocks in the centre of a downfaulted block.

Reverse and Thrust Faults — Compressional Stress

A reverse fault forms when compressional stress drives the hanging wall upward relative to the footwall. This is the opposite of a normal fault. Reverse faults have steep fault planes, typically dipping at 45° or more.

When the fault plane is very shallow — dipping at less than 30° — the structure is specifically called a thrust fault. Thrust faults are spectacular: compressional stress can push entire sheets of older rock many kilometres over younger rocks. The Moine Thrust in north-west Scotland is a famous example, where ancient Precambrian rocks were thrust horizontally over younger Cambrian strata during the Caledonian orogeny. The diagnostic field observation is finding older rocks sitting directly on top of younger ones — apparently the “wrong way round” by the law of superposition.

Examiner reports consistently flag this mix-up. The key is the word “normal” — it refers to what happens normally under gravity: the hanging wall slips down. A reverse fault is the reverse of that — the hanging wall moves up. In a diagram, check: if the rocks on the left side of the fault appear to have moved upward, the left block is the hanging wall and it has gone up — reverse fault. If it has gone down — normal fault. Practise sketching both types with arrows showing the hanging-wall movement direction.

Strike-Slip Faults — Shear Stress

A strike-slip fault forms when shear stress causes the two sides of a fault to slide horizontally past each other. There is little or no vertical movement. Strike-slip faults are associated with conservative plate boundaries, where two plates grind sideways past each other. The San Andreas Fault in California is the world’s most studied strike-slip fault: the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year.

On a geological map, strike-slip faults are identified by the sideways offset of rock units, dykes, or other linear features that cross the fault. If you face the fault and the block on the other side has moved to the right, it is called a dextral (right-lateral) fault. If it has moved to the left, it is sinistral (left-lateral). Identifying the offset of a distinctive marker — such as a dyke displaced by a fault — is a common exam question on the practical-skills component.

Key Fact

Normal fault → tensional stress, hanging wall down (divergent boundaries). Reverse/thrust fault → compressional stress, hanging wall up (convergent boundaries). Strike-slip fault → shear stress, horizontal movement (conservative boundaries).

When a fault cuts across a series of rock units on a map, the units appear displaced — they start on one side of the fault line and continue at a different position on the other. For a normal or reverse fault, the displacement is vertical: units on the downthrown side are lower. For a strike-slip fault, units are shifted sideways. The amount of shift is called the fault displacement. You can calculate horizontal displacement by measuring the offset of a marker horizon on the map and applying the map scale. Always include units (metres or kilometres) in your answer.

Faults and Earthquakes

Faults are geologically active as long as the stress driving them continues. Movement is rarely smooth — blocks lock together until stress overcomes friction, then slip rapidly, releasing energy as seismic waves. This is the mechanism of most earthquakes. The zone of crushed and ground-up rock along the fault plane is called fault breccia. Deep faults that cut right through the lithosphere are particularly significant because they control the location of volcanic activity and earthquake zones, both of which you will meet in the plate boundaries lesson.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark compare question on faults, you must mention both features in each comparison — not just describe one fault. For example: “In a normal fault the hanging wall moves downward, whereas in a reverse fault the hanging wall moves upward.” Missing the comparison word (whereas/while/by contrast) is the most common reason students score 2 out of 4. For map questions, trace the displacement of a named rock unit or dyke across the fault line to justify your identification.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Faults are fractures in rock along which displacement has occurred. The hanging wall is above the fault plane; the footwall is below.
  • Normal faults (hanging wall down, tensional stress) form at divergent boundaries; reverse and thrust faults (hanging wall up, compressional stress) at convergent boundaries; strike-slip faults (horizontal movement, shear stress) at conservative boundaries.
  • Fault type is identified from the direction of displacement, the stress context, and map evidence such as the offset of rock units or dykes.

practice_questions.text:
In which type of fault does the hanging wall move downward relative to the footwall?
A) Reverse fault
B) Thrust fault
C) Normal fault
D) Strike-slip fault
Name the type of tectonic stress that produces a strike-slip fault.
Describe two differences between a normal fault and a reverse fault.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (2 per comparison, 1 for naming the difference, 1 for giving both sides):
• Normal fault: hanging wall moves down; reverse fault: hanging wall moves up [2]
• Normal fault: produced by tensional stress; reverse fault: produced by compressional stress [2]
Accept: normal fault typical at divergent boundary; reverse fault typical at convergent boundary [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a thrust fault forms and why it can result in older rocks lying above younger rocks.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Compressional stress squeezes the crust [1]
• The fault plane is at a low angle (less than 30°) and the hanging wall is pushed horizontally over the footwall [1]
• Older rocks on the hanging wall are thrust over younger rocks on the footwall, reversing the normal order of superposition [1]

practice_questions.text: A geologist identifies a strike-slip fault on a geological map. A vertical dolerite dyke that was originally continuous is now displaced 200 m to the right across the fault. The map scale is 1:25,000. Calculate the actual displacement and state what type of strike-slip movement this represents.
practice_questions.marks: Displacement: 200 m [already given as actual distance in this example — accept the identification part for 1 mark]. Dextral (right-lateral) movement [1 mark]. If the student needs to convert from map distance: 200 m stated directly = 200 m actual displacement [1 mark for calculation, 1 mark for dextral].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the evidence a geologist would use to distinguish between a normal fault and a reverse fault when examining a geological map and cross-section. Consider the evidence available and any limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly explains map evidence (direction of displacement of rock units, which side is downthrown) and cross-section evidence (hanging wall up or down, fault plane dip angle); links to stress type at plate boundaries; evaluates limitations (fault plane obscured by later deposits; erosion removes displaced units; vertical faults cannot be distinguished as normal or reverse without a cross-section). Balanced conclusion.
Secure: Correctly identifies at least two pieces of map or cross-section evidence for each fault type; notes at least one limitation; some evaluative language.
Developing: Identifies one piece of evidence for one fault type; limited comparison or evaluation.
Emerging: Shows partial understanding of one fault type; little evaluation.

The block of rock that lies above the fault plane.

flashcard_questions.q: In a normal fault, which direction does the hanging wall move?
What stress produces a normal fault?
In a reverse fault, which direction does the hanging wall move?
What stress produces a reverse fault?
What is the key difference between a thrust fault and a reverse fault?
flashcard_questions.a: A thrust fault has a low-angle fault plane (less than 30°); a reverse fault is steep.

flashcard_questions.q: What geological observation proves a thrust fault has occurred?
flashcard_questions.a: Older rocks sitting directly on top of younger rocks.

What stress produces a strike-slip fault?
The San Andreas Fault is an example of which fault type?
If the block on the far side of a strike-slip fault has moved to the right, what is the fault called?

glossary_terms.definition: A planar fracture in rock along which the two sides have moved relative to each other.
The block of rock that lies above the fault plane.
The block of rock that lies below the fault plane.
A fault in which the hanging wall has moved downward relative to the footwall, produced by tensional stress.
A type of tectonic stress that pulls rock apart, stretching and thinning the crust.
A fault in which the hanging wall has moved upward relative to the footwall, produced by compressional stress.
A low-angle reverse fault along which older rocks have been pushed horizontally over younger rocks for many kilometres.
A fault in which the two blocks move horizontally past each other in opposite directions along the fault plane.
A type of tectonic stress that acts parallel to a surface, causing one block to slide past another.
